title: A New Name for Zion: My Delight Is in Her
summary: The speaker refuses to keep silent until Jerusalem's righteousness shines and the nations see her glory. She will receive a new name: no longer Forsaken and Desolate, but Hephzibah and Beulah, because the LORD delights in her and will rejoice over her as a bridegroom over his bride. Watchmen are posted on her walls to give God no rest until he establishes her, God swears that her harvests will never again be taken by enemies, and the people are told to prepare the highway because her Savior is coming.
story: Chapter 62 completes the bright center of Isaiah's final section (chapters 60 to 62). Chapter 60 described Zion's glory, chapter 61 the anointed one who brings it, and chapter 62 a voice of relentless intercession that will not rest until the promise is fulfilled. The chapter gathers threads from across the book: the marriage imagery of chapter 54, the highway of 40:3 and 57:14, the watchmen of 52:8, and the announcement that God's reward is with him from 40:10. After it, chapter 63 turns abruptly to the LORD returning from judgment and to the people's lament, showing that the promised glory has not yet fully arrived.
historical: For the returned exiles in Judah, the names Forsaken and Desolate would have described what they saw every day. Jerusalem remained partly in ruins for decades after the return; Nehemiah 1 and 2 describe its walls broken down and gates burned, as late as the mid-fifth century BC. The promise in verses 8 and 9 that enemies would no longer eat Judah's grain spoke to a people who had watched foreign armies and later imperial taxes take the fruit of their labor (compare Nehemiah 5:4, where people borrowed to pay the king's tax, and Nehemiah 9:36-37). The speaker who will not keep silent is not named. He may be the prophet, the anointed one of chapter 61, or God himself, and interpreters differ.
cultural:
Names mattered in ancient Israel. They described character, circumstances, or hopes, and a change of name marked a change of identity, as with Abram to Abraham and Jacob to Israel (Genesis 17:5; 32:28). Hephzibah, meaning my delight is in her, was a real name: it was the name of the mother of King Manasseh (2 Kings 21:1). Beulah means married. In a society where an unmarried or abandoned woman had little security, to be called married was to be called protected, provided for, and honored.

Watchmen stood on city walls to look out for danger or messengers, calling out news day and night. Here they become intercessors who call on the LORD continually. The highway of verse 10 and the raised banner evoke preparations for a royal arrival or a great procession, when roads were cleared of stones and flags signaled the route. The harvest promise of verses 8 and 9 recalls the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28:33, which warned that a foreign nation would eat the produce of Israel's land.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1 to 5 are spoken by a voice determined not to keep silent, and they culminate in the new names and the marriage image: as a young man marries a young woman, so your sons will marry you, a daring metaphor for the land being possessed and cherished again. Verses 6 to 9 turn to the watchmen and God's oath, sworn by his right hand. Verses 10 to 12 are a closing summons to prepare the way, ending with a final cascade of new names for the people and the city. The chapter is framed by silence refused (verse 1) and a city no longer forsaken (verse 12).

outline.t: I will not keep silent: new names and a wedding
Watchmen on the walls: give God no rest
God's oath: your harvest will be your own
Prepare the way: your Savior comes

doctrines.note: The watchmen are to give the LORD no rest until he establishes Jerusalem (verses 6 and 7). Persistent prayer is not an attempt to change God's mind but an agreement with his promise, pressing for its fulfillment.
The marriage image and God's sworn oath (verse 8) express covenant faithfulness at its warmest. God does not merely tolerate his people; he delights in them and rejoices over them.
The chapter names a future in which the forsaken are sought out and the desolate are married. Hope in Scripture includes the giving of a new identity by God himself.

words.note: Hephzibah, my delight is in her, formed from the verb chaphets, to take pleasure in. The name is God's declaration of affection for his city, replacing the name Forsaken. That it was also the name of a queen mother in Judah (2 Kings 21:1) shows it was a name a family might give a beloved daughter.

Baal, to marry. It appears in Beulah (married) and in verse 5, where your sons will marry you. The same root named the Canaanite god Baal and means lord or owner. In Isaiah it is reclaimed for the LORD's covenant love, as in 54:5, where your Maker is your husband.

Yesha, salvation, deliverance. “Her salvation like a blazing torch” (verse 1) and “your Savior comes” in verse 11 (literally your salvation comes) use the root from which the name Joshua, and its Greek form Jesus, is built. The chapter's final announcement is that salvation is personal: he is coming.

christ: Matthew's account of Jesus's entry into Jerusalem joins the opening words of verse 11, say to the Daughter of Zion, with Zechariah 9:9 (Matthew 21:5), presenting Jesus as the Savior coming to the city. The marriage imagery of verses 4 and 5 becomes the New Testament's picture of Christ and the church: Christ loves the church as a husband (Ephesians 5:25-27), and the new Jerusalem comes down as a bride adorned for her husband (Revelation 21:2). The promise of a new name recurs in Revelation 2:17 and 3:12. The chapter's own focus is Zion; the New Testament extends it to the people gathered around the Messiah, Jew and Gentile together.
questions: The names Forsaken and Desolate are replaced by names of delight. What names have you carried that God might want to replace?
The watchmen are told to give God no rest. What promise of God might you pray for with that kind of persistence?
How does it change your view of God to read that he rejoices over his people as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride?
